title: AlphaGenome informed machine learning for pathogenicity prediction of germline mutations
summary: Accurate interpretation of germline variants remains a central challenge in clinical genomics. Existing in silico pathogenicity predictors often provide incomplete coverage or restricted to missense variants from the coding region, leaving the variants from splice sites, -UTR, and intronic regions under-scored. We present AGVarPred, a gradient-boosted classifier designed to predict the pathogenicity of germline mutants, with a broad consequence-class coverage across SNVs and indels. Here, the population allele frequency from gnomAD, functional consequence annotations from Ensembl VEP, and cell-type-specific functional genomic scores from the AlphaGenome platform were integrated to develop the classifier. Using a gene-level split of 134,002 high-confidence ClinVar variants across 9,222 genes, AGVarPred achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.9753 (95% CI 0.9731-0.9775) and a AUC-PR of 0.9606 on 12,385 scored internal test variants. A paired DeLong analysis showed that the full model significantly outperformed an allele-frequency-plus-VEP model ({Delta}AUC = 0.1539, 95% CI 0.1489-0.1589; p < 1 x 10-300), supporting a substantial incremental contribution from AlphaGenome-derived features. Performance remained strong when restricted to SNVs (AUC-ROC 0.9558) and was also high for indels (AUC-ROC 0.9532). On five external benchmarks, AUC-ROCs ranged from 0.528 on a functional-assay-derived benchmark to 0.977 on a clinically curated deafness database, reflecting its dependence on benchmark composition and label source. A separate analysis of the VIP Database, whose pathogenic labels are ClinVar-derived, showed consistent performance (AUC-ROC of 0.892) in held-out genes. AGVarPred scored 100% of evaluated variants in the external benchmarks, whereas AlphaMissense and REVEL covered only small fractions of non-missense variants. Model interpretation indicated that gnomAD allele frequency was the dominant individual predictor; the 111 AlphaGenome features provided complementary functional signal, with splicing and chromatin assays contributing to the largest share of the AlphaGenome SHAP mass. A web-based interface for AGVarPred is available at https://pankaj357.github.io/AGVarPred/ to facilitate the submission of normalized GRCh38 germline variants and retrieval of pathogenicity predictions using the frozen AGVarPred model.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Structural Prioritization of Sulforaphane Targets in Neurodegeneration: A Multi-Dataset In Silico Study
summary: Sulforaphane (SFN), a natural isothiocyanate from cruciferous vegetables, exerts neuroprotective effects through mechanisms extending beyond canonical Nrf2/ARE activation. Here, we developed a multi-dataset computational framework integrating transcriptomic analysis, multi-criteria target prioritization, and structural docking evaluation. R- and S-SFN were docked against 693 prioritized targets using AutoDock Vina, followed by cross-validation, brain expression profiling, and molecular dynamics simulations. Four genes (IGSF9, KCNQ5, KCTD12, and NFIX) were dysregulated across all four datasets. Among 693 targets, 88 showed favorable predicted docking scores (deltaG less than or equal to -4.0 kcal/mol), with 65 (73.9%) exhibiting expression in at least one GTEx brain region. Independent cross-validation showed significant enrichment of prioritized targets in an SFN-responsive Alzheimer disease transcriptomic dataset (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.08-1.89, p = 0.0104). Complementary disease gene set enrichment confirmed that 33% of strong hits (29/88) overlap established neurodegeneration gene sets across AD, PD, and ALS - including ACHE, target of FDA-approved anti-AD drugs - with highly significant enrichment across all three disease categories (OR range: 67-127, all p less than 0.001). R-SFN showed a modest but statistically detectable preference over S-SFN across the 88 strong hits (Wilcoxon p = 0.0081; paired t-test p = 0.0047). TMEM45A, GRIK2, and FABP3 emerged as putative neurodegeneration-relevant targets. Molecular dynamics simulations supported the structural stability of R-SFN poses for TMEM45A, GRIK2, and FABP3, while MM-GBSA estimated favorable binding energies for GRIK2 (deltaG_bind = -19.78 kcal/mol) and FABP3 (deltaG_bind = -14.49 kcal/mol). These findings generate testable hypotheses regarding previously underexplored molecular targets that may contribute to the neuroprotective actions of SFN.

title: A Pipeline for Predicting Variant Associations with Complex Disorders via Functional Annotations
summary: The study of complex disorders is limited by the lack of structured data sets that integrate genetic association signals with rich functional annotations. While genome wide association studies (GWAS) provide large collections of associated variants, these are heterogeneous, studydependent, and not directly suitable for machine learning applications. Although frameworks such as Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) offer comprehensive variant-level features, there is no standardised procedure to construct curated, balanced, and reproducible data sets for the systematic study of complex traits. We introduce a scalable and reproducible pipeline for generating CADD-annotated variant data sets associated with complex disorders defined via Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO) terms. The pipeline integrates GWAS summary statistics, genome mapping, chromosomestratified negative sampling, and large-scale annotation, while addressing class imbalance and feature redundancy. The resulting data sets provide curated, balanced, and annotation-rich representations of variant-trait associations, suitable for statistical learning, systematic model evaluation and comparison, and analysis of functional annotation contributions and interactions.

title: Accelerated discovery and optimization of a potent andselective MMP12 inhibitor with the machine learningplatform CAMOLE-1
summary: Machine learning techniques are being readily utilized to accelerate drug discovery pipelines. Peptide therapeutics are an emerging modality that offer the advantage of increased potency with reduced toxicity that are amenable to machine learning discovery and optimization. This work describes the Calico All-Atom Molecule Engine (CAMOLE-1), a machine learning platform for de novo peptide inhibitor design. CAMOLE-1 incorporates an all-atom diffusion model that enables rapid non-canonical peptide discovery and optimization, and integrates physics based computational filtering, and biochemical testing. We applied CAMOLE-1 towards the discovery of peptide inhibitors of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), a target class that has essentially evaded therapeutic development. Starting from canonical amino acid-based design, an MMP12 peptide inhibitor was identified and further optimized to improve potency. From these initial peptides, we used our all-atom diffusion model to determine a predicted structure, allowing us to design a potent and selective inhibitor over the course of about one year and 270 synthesized peptides. Predicted structures of both canonical and non-canonical peptide inhibitors showed high fidelity to our experimentally determined peptide-bound crystal structures. To our knowledge, this is the first described effort to use machine learning techniques to iteratively drive peptide inhibitor design beyond initial hit discovery into the development of selective, potent lead peptide inhibitors with improved pharmacokinetic properties. Our study illustrates the power of machine learning-driven design of peptide inhibitors, an exciting emerging therapeutic modality.
